title: SYSK’s Summer Movie Playlist: Some Movies That Changed Filmmaking
summary: Summer movie playlist rerun of a February 2015 Stuff You Should Know episode on films that changed filmmaking, from the earliest movies through Star Wars-era innovations. Chuck introduces it as part of the playlist. Josh and the co-host (credited as iHeart Intro in the transcript) walk through Lumière's Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory, Battleship Potemkin and Soviet montage and the Odessa Steps, Buster Keaton's stunts and deadpan style, The Jazz Singer and Vitaphone synced sound, Citizen Kane's deep focus, low angles and nonlinear storytelling, Breathless and the French New Wave with jump cuts, Fellini's 8½ and surrealism, Toy Story as the first all-CGI feature, and 2001: A Space Odyssey with Kubrick's pacing, match cut, and influence on Star Wars and Ridley Scott. The episode also covers Fatty Arbuckle as a correction, a listener mail about scientific law versus theory, and a discussion of Birdman and Foxcatcher.

segments.title: Opening and rerun introduction
segments.summary: Chuck introduces this rerun from the Summer Movie Playlist, an episode from February 2015 on movies that changed filmmaking, and the show's opening credits play.

segments.title: Banter about movies, Ebert documentary, and the studio move
segments.summary: The hosts joke about movie-watching habits, the Roger Ebert documentary Life Itself, and the last episode in the old studio before the move.

segments.title: Battleship Potemkin and Soviet montage
segments.summary: The hosts discuss Lumière's 1895 short Workers Leaving the Lumière Factory as the first film, then Battleship Potemkin (1925), a silent Soviet propaganda narrative about a 1905 mutiny. They cover its banning, Soviet montage theory, and the Odessa Steps sequence, whose baby carriage and glasses shots were echoed in later films.

segments.title: Buster Keaton and deadpan stunts
segments.summary: The hosts describe Buster Keaton's dangerous stunts, including the falling house scene in Steamboat Bill Jr. (named by the hosts as a film), and his deadpan style contrasted with Charlie Chaplin. They discuss his influence on later deadpan performers, and Josh corrects an earlier remark about Fatty Arbuckle, noting he was acquitted.

segments.title: The Jazz Singer and early synchronized sound
segments.summary: The 1927 The Jazz Singer is discussed as the first feature with substantial spoken dialogue, using Vitaphone discs synced to the projector. It grossed about three and a half million dollars and was ineligible for Best Picture.

segments.title: Citizen Kane and nonlinear storytelling
segments.summary: Citizen Kane (1941) is presented as a landmark for its nonlinear narrative, deep focus by Greg Toland, off-center framing, expressionistic lighting, low-angle shots, and the star wipe. Orson Welles's theater background is noted, and Fritz Lang is named as a pioneer of nonlinear structure in the hosts' discussion.

segments.title: Breathless and the French New Wave
segments.summary: Chuck explains the French New Wave, including Breathless (Godard) with its handheld camera, flat performances, and use of jump cuts, which were jarring at the time. The hosts note Wes Anderson's debt to the movement and Scorsese's jump cuts in Goodfellas.

segments.title: Fellini's 8½ and surrealist filmmaking
segments.summary: Fellini's 8½ is introduced as a movie about making movies starring Marcello Mastroianni, with a dream sequence of a car in traffic that inspired surrealist filmmaking. Its traffic-jam opening is compared to Falling Down and to R.E.M.'s Everybody Hurts video, and the hosts discuss Falling Down's flaws.

segments.title: Sponsor break and jingle credits
segments.summary: A break is taken, then the hosts credit the original jingle creator and a cover artist who remixed it, and mention the Sheepdogs' tour.

segments.title: Toy Story and the rise of CGI animation
segments.summary: Toy Story (1995) is described as the first all-CGI feature and a game changer. The hosts discuss The Adventures of Tintin's animation, the loss of cell animation, The Iron Giant, and the Academy Best Animated Feature category, noting Up was also nominated for Best Picture.

segments.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey and Kubrick
segments.summary: 2001: A Space Odyssey is discussed for its technical achievement, Kubrick's obsessive detail, and its science-fact approach developed with Arthur C. Clarke and Carl Sagan. George Lucas's comment that 2001 was the better movie than Star Wars is mentioned. The hosts compare it to Interstellar and Inception.

segments.title: 2001 structure, match cut, and Kubrick's production secrets
segments.summary: The hosts discuss the three movements of 2001, the bone-to-satellite match cut (which depicts a nuclear warhead), HAL 9000, alternate titles, the Room 237 documentary, and Kubrick's destruction of sets, props, and footage. They say they could do a podcast on Kubrick.

segments.title: Related episodes and site pointers
segments.summary: Josh mentions related episodes on exploitation films, James Bond, and Cannonball Run, and tells listeners how to find them in the archive.

segments.title: Listener mail: scientific law vs. theory, and Birdman and Foxcatcher
segments.summary: A listener named Mike DuPont writes that a scientific theory is more developed than a law, and that law describes what happens while theory explains why. The hosts then discuss Birdman and Foxcatcher, with Josh criticizing Birdman's pretentious tone and ending.

segments.title: Outro and contact info
segments.summary: Josh gives contact information for the show, including Twitter, Facebook, email, and the website, and the credits play.
